papers.abstract: We address the task of long-video, camera-controlled generation from a single image. The dominant autoregressive paradigm suffers from two key limitations: (1) error accumulation over time, as distant frames are conditioned on previously generated outputs rather than ground truth, leading to drift; and (2) ambiguity in how to incorporate camera control. Standard solutions to both--such as self-forcing and conditioning on explicit 6-DOF poses--either incur significant computational overhead or produce drifting scene geometries over time. We propose a simple and lightweight framework that combines autoregressive generation (WanAR) with hierarchical long-context denoising (FixAR). To enforce scene geometry remains consistent with input cameras, we draw from feed-forward novel-view synthesis and reformulate video generation as a warping-and-inpainting problem. To mitigate drift, we introduce a hierarchical denoising strategy in which different stages condition on different temporal histories. Specifically, we first generate frames conditioned on the immediate past, and then refine them using a second denoiser conditioned on a temporally subsampled long-range history to enforce global consistency. This fine-to-coarse scheme enables each generated frame to effectively condition on the full temporal context without incurring a prohibitive cost. Experiments on RealEstate10k and DL3DV demonstrate that WanAR+FixAR outperforms prior methods for camera-controlled long-video generation, producing results that are both temporally stable and consistent with input camera trajectories.
authors: Kaihua Chen, Yiming Gong, Deva Ramanan, Tarasha Khurana
bullets: Targets error accumulation and ambiguous camera-control conditioning in long autoregressive video generation.
Recasts generation as a camera-guided warping-and-inpainting problem to preserve scene geometry.
Uses immediate temporal history for initial generation and subsampled long-range history for refinement.
Evaluated on RealEstate10k and DL3DV, where it outperforms prior methods in temporal stability and camera-trajectory consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WanAR, FixAR, and InterpolatAR. We build upon WAN Team et al. (2025), a video diffusion model, and adapt it for camera-controlled autoregressive video generation in static 3D scenes. All three stages share the same Wan2.1 backbone weights, with a different stage-specific LoRA checkpoint loaded for each stage. At each rollout, we estimate depth using MoGe-2 Wang et al. (2025c) on the input frame (or the last generated frame from the previous rollout), and warp it into future camera poses to provide geometry-aware conditioning for WanAR (top). While WanAR can generate plausible long videos autoregressively, visual drift and artifacts gradually accumulate over multiple rollouts. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a hierarchical denoising framework with a second-stage denoiser, FixAR (middle), which refines temporally subsampled keyframes generated across different rollouts using a broader temporal context. Finally, since FixAR only operates on sparse keyframes, we apply InterpolatAR to synthesize intermediate frames between adjacent refined keyframes (bottom). The entire three-stage pipeline can itself be rolled out autoregressively to further extend the video. This hierarchical fine-to-coarse formulation enables both accurate camera control and temporally stable long-horizon video generation.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10k and DL3DV. We show qualitative results on two test scene from RealEstate10k (top two examples) and DL3DV (bottom two examples) across a range of video generation, and novel-view synthesis baselines. We see that proposed WanAR + FixAR combination of models “renders” the scene using scale-consistent camera poses (as compared to ray encoding in DFoT or Plucker conditioning in LingBot), and show that hierarchical denoising mitigates drift over time which some autoregressive baselines like VMem struggle with. We also note that TrajectoryCrafter, a method designed for novel-view synthesis (in short sequences) is also surprisingly strong at the task of camera-controlled minute-long video generation.

Figure 1: In this work, we consider the problem of camera-controlled video generation. Existing approaches condition on cameras represented as ray encodings or Plucker coordinates, but these learn poses up to a global scale factor. We draw from literature in feed-forward novel-view synthesis that warp given views into future poses and reformulate video generation as video inpainting (left). While this allows for precise camera control, minute-long autoregressive video generation in this setup still suffers from drift and error accumulation over time. We propose a hierarchical denoising scheme (right) that looks at multiple rollouts from the inpainting stage and corrects for long horizon artifacts.

Figure 6: We identify a key limitation of existing camera-conditioned methods. When explicit 6- DOF poses are used as conditioning—e.g., via Plücker coordinates or ray maps Song et al. (2025); Team et al. (2026b)—it is difficult to enforce a consistent scale between the scene and the camera trajectory. As a result, generated videos may exhibit visual inconsistencies (top), reflecting scenes rendered under an arbitrary pose scale. Importantly, standard camera-control metrics Xiao et al. (2025) perform a scale alignment with ground-truth camera poses prior to evaluation. Consequently, even when predicted camera trajectories are incorrect up to a global scale factor, they can still achieve low error (bottom), masking this failure mode. Current methods evaluating performance with the PSNR metric circumvent this issue, as they overfit to the pose distribution in a particular datasets, which indicates their limited generalization to other scene or camera trajectories. In our approach, we mitigate this issue by aligning MoGE depth predictions to ground-truth depth for each rollout, and by adopting a warping-and-inpainting formulation for long-video generation. We also adopt novel-view synthesis protocols for evaluation, and instead benchmark methods for camera-control with the masked PSNR (mPSNR) metric.

Figure 5: Top-k evaluation. We note that generative methods for camera-controlled video generation can produce multi-modal outputs for unseen regions of the scene as camera pans in new direction. We conduct such an evaluation for our method. Our finding is that the performance of our final predictions improves with respect to the ground-truth as more samples are drawn from WanAR (thereby covering the generation of multiple plausible 3D scenes in the future).
Figure 4: Qualitative analysis of hierarchical denoising. WanAR exhibits drift over long rollouts, while FixAR mitigates the drift and cleans up accumulated artifacts.

Table 5: Computational cost comparison with baselines. Runtime and peak GPU memory are measured on 280-frame RealEstate10K videos using a single 80GB H100 GPU. We also report our method at 480× 832× 49 for a resolution-matched comparison.

Table 2: Comparison to state-of-the-art on DL3DV Ling et al. (2024). We compare our method with prior art on the DL3DV dataset which has more challenging camera motion, like sudden translation changes, and 360◦ camera pan. Despite this, our method outperforms baselines by a considerable margin. Once again, mPSNR demonstrates better camera control with our warp-and-inpaint strategy for long video generation.

Table 1: Comparison to state-of-the-art on RealEstate10K Zhou et al. (2018). We compare our hierarchical diffusion strategy to state-of-the-art approaches for long video generation and novelview synthesis of static scenes. Our first finding is that a combination of WanAR + FixAR beats all prior art on RealEstate10K, which we attribute to better camera control in WanAR, and better drift mitigation from FixAR. One surprising finding is that novel-view synthesis approaches like TrajectoryCrafter in fact perform better at this task than many long video generation works. With mPSNR, we show better retention of visible regions particularly driven by precise camera control.

Table 7: Comparison of different geometry estimation methods. We initialize WanAR using the first-frame depth estimated by each method and report performance after one rollout. Results are similar across estimators, indicating limited sensitivity to the choice of depth estimator.

Table 6: Ablation on FixAR keyframe interval and sequence length. We compare 49-frame and 25-frame FixAR variants under different keyframe intervals. The 49-frame model remains stable across its training range, while larger intervals degrade the performance of the 25-frame model.
Table 4: Comparison of different conditioning strategies. The Plucker baseline adds a convolutional adapter to the Wan2.1-14B backbone, and is finetuned on Re10K using the same setup.
Table 3: Quantitative analysis of hierarchical denoising. FixAR improves generation realism and leads to consistent gains across evaluation metrics.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation for autoregressive (AR) video generation commonly first initializes an AR student and then refines it with distribution matching distillation (DMD). This refinement process faces two challenges. First, although initialization already yields a reasonably capable student, DMD obtains the refinement direction indirectly by estimating the full student score before forming the teacher-student correction. Second, detached-history training prevents the generator from assigning credit to a current chunk for its influence on subsequent chunks. We introduce Leta, a few-step distillation framework that addresses these challenges with ScoreDelta and FutureCredit. ScoreDelta directly estimates the teacher-student correction from denoising residuals, while FutureCredit learns an auxiliary cross-chunk update signal from vector-Jacobian products (VJPs) of next-chunk teacher residuals. Leta combines these signals into a joint teacher-guided update field in a single forward pass during generator updates. Teacher evaluations and credit VJPs are used only for estimator training. For ScoreDelta, we establish population equivalence to score-difference estimation and a conditional approximation advantage under limited capacity in a fixed-feature linear model. In our controlled experiments, Leta improves over DMD by 0.9 points on VBench and 0.66 on VideoAlign. This advantage persists at a higher generator update frequency (a generator-to-estimator update ratio of G:E=1:1), where Leta improves over DMD by 1.6 on VBench and 0.35 on VideoAlign. Project page: https://scdzx.github.io/Leta/.
authors: Zixuan Duan, Yabo Chen, Xunzhi Xiang, Xin Zhang, Haibin Huang, Yin Chen, Chi Zhang, Qi Fan

papers.abstract: While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts. Project page is here: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing
authors: Zelin Gao, Hao Ouyang, Jiapeng Zhu, Qiuyu Wang, Jingye Chen, Zichen Liu, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu

Applies consistency and distribution-matching distillation to produce a four-step autoregressive generator.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality, event following, and camera control, with high-fidelity rollouts lasting up to one hour on reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generation enables low-latency streaming, yet prevailing training pipelines separate causal adaptation from distribution matching. Recent representation-based text-to-video methods retain this separation by starting from ODE-initialized checkpoints, even when the target distribution is defined directly by reference videos. We introduce Direct Forcing, a single-stage framework that uses reference videos both as paired examples of how a history continues and as a target population for self-generated rollouts. Causal Continuation Alignment learns paired spatiotemporal correspondence under reference histories, while Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to align the representation distributions of self-generated and reference videos. Together, these complementary signals allow a pretrained video model to learn causal continuation and the target video distribution in a single training stage. Dynamic Gradient Balancing adapts the relative gradient contributions of continuation alignment and distribution matching during training. Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Direct Forcing learns a four-step autoregressive generator in 250 updates without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision, achieving 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of dynamic gradient balancing and reveal distinct representation preferences: deeper features benefit continuation alignment, whereas intermediate features yield better performance for rollout distribution matching.
authors: Haojun Xu, Jie Huang, Xin Lu, Mingchen Zhong, Zihao Fan, Linjiang Huang, Si Liu

Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, it trains a four-step generator in 250 updates without separate initialization or online diffusion-score supervision.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
authors: Ruopeng Gao, Yukun Huang, Jiarui Hu, Shuai Wang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Limin Wang
bullets: Teacher forcing can exploit temporal redundancy, favoring local continuity over genuine modeling of visual evolution.
FCP adds an auxiliary future-chunk prediction objective alongside teacher-forced denoising.

It improves physical plausibility while using less overall training compute than standard teacher-forced training.
Visualizations suggest FCP produces a more structured representation space, potentially benefiting autoregressive world models.

papers.abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.
authors: Jihai Zhang, Runjia Qian, Kaiqin Kong, Biao Jiang, Puyi Wang, Siru Chen, Tianle Li, Guanjie Chen, Junyi Wu, Chubin Chen, Yuanhang Li, Kaichen Huang, Haobo Zhang, Yangguang Li, Wei Yu, Guibin Chen, Yu Cheng, Yahui Zhou
bullets: Addresses the gap between controllable video generation and playable worlds requiring persistent state, executable rules, and low-latency interaction.

Separates game execution from visual generation: an engine manages state and mechanics, while an autoregressive video model renders detailed visuals from low-poly proxies, captions, and memory references.
A multimodal coding agent converts player ideas into game code and dynamic scene descriptions.
Demonstrates customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics.
Achieves 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on an RTX5090 with 112 ms key-press-to-display latency; code, weights, and assets are released.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Architecture of the rendering model. The noisy latent of one chunk (one latent frame, four video frames) and the low-poly proxy encoded by TAEHV are concatenated into 148 channels and patchified into 405 tokens per latent frame at 480×864. Thirty causal DiT blocks apply self-attention over a KV cache that holds spatial-memory frames, reference frames, and the latest 20 chunks, cross-attention to the cached text keys and values of the dynamic caption, and a feed-forward network, each modulated by the timestep through AdaLN. The output head predicts a velocity, one or two flow updates produce the clean latent, and TAEHV decodes four frames. The finished chunk is then re-run at t = 0 without the control input to write its keys and values into the cache.

Figure 6: Overview of the inference optimizations. (a) Per-block GPU time on an RTX 5090, broken down by kernel category. (b) Decoding is moved ahead of the clean-KV update, so frames are output earlier. (c) Instead of shifting the whole KV window at every step, the ring cache writes the new frame into the oldest slot. (d) Self-attention is split into seven window ranges whose quantized keys and values are cached; the partial outputs are combined by log-sum-exp.

Figure 2: Roadmap of Matrix-Game V4: The multimodal coding agent and the game engine form the harness for the video generation model. The player sends ideas and requests to the agent and actions to the engine (1). The agent writes the world, turning ideas into game code and scenes for the engine, and translates the world, turning the state and events reported by the engine into text descriptions. The engine maintains the world state and the rules in code (2) and sends control signals as a structural rendering of the scene (3). The video generation model renders frames in real time from the text description, its past frames, and the structural rendering (4). The generated frame returns to the player as visual feedback (5).

Figure 4: Dynamic captions follow the engine state. Top: low-poly proxy frames of one CitySample driving clip; numbered markers are the visible objects that the engine reports for this frame, each linked by its instance ID to a semantic description. Below: the caption that the rule-based template produces for the same frame, without any vision-language model. Orange text comes from object states and events, and blue text from object positions and distances. As the car moves, parked vehicles leave the description, pedestrians change from standing to approaching, and newly visible objects are announced under “Changes”.

Figure 8: Game modes written with the coding agent, rendered in real time. Top: in the thirdperson shooter, the agent adds health and ammunition control, shield durability, a faster shotgun, a game-over condition, and simple sound effects. Middle: in the driving game, the agent implements a time trial with route checkpoints and collision penalties. Bottom: the same driving game turned into a pursuit mode, in which the player must intercept a target vehicle and stay close to it for five seconds. The engine evaluates every rule; the video model renders each frame from the engine output.

Figure 7: Re-rendering over 40-second held-out rollouts. For each game, the upper row is the low-poly proxy from the engine and the lower row is the frame generated by the distilled causal model at the same time step. The generated frames follow the proxy layout, camera, and object motion throughout the rollout, while the model fills in materials, vegetation, lighting, smoke, and muzzle effects.

(b) For every 81-frame clip, frame-aligned CSV records of camera pose, actions, visible objects, events, and environment are turned into a prompt: visible object IDs are looked up in a description table, spatial and temporal cues are composed, and a template produces the clip prompt.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.
authors: Yuanyu He, Zhuokun Chen, Yefei He, Zhiwei Tang, Jiasheng Tang, Yinghao Yu, Jianfei Cai, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and memory usage of dense autoregressive video diffusion.
Separates dynamic and static regions to exploit temporal redundancy in videos.
Compresses historical KV caches by retaining dynamic features and allocates computation according to localized motion.
Uses dynamics-guided distillation to improve performance with lightweight training.
On VBench, achieves 2.16× faster generation while maintaining high visual fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of the proposed framework. We introduce a unified approach to optimize AR diffusion generation for both storage and computational efficiency. Storage Management (Left): Tokens from historical chunks are selectively cached in memory based on a layer-wise threshold σl, discarding redundant information. The final frame of the immediately preceding chunk serves as a reference frame, with all its tokens unconditionally preserved. Computation Optimization (Right): This reference frame acts as an anchor to guide token selection for the current chunkC . Redundant tokens are filtered out via a threshold γ to reduce computational overhead. AR Diffusion Generation (Middle): Finally, the retained historical tokens from memory and the active tokens from the current chunk are concatenated and processed by the AR diffusion.

Figure 1: Spatiotemporal dynamic analysis of video generation under different motion priors (left: camera panning; right: subject motion). (a) Real-world scenes. The videos are synthesized via Self Forcing, conditioned on a single text prompt provided at the initialization stage. (b) Attention distributions. Visualizations reveal the distribution of temporal attention scores, indicating that the generation process predominantly focuses on active dynamic elements alongside adjacent temporal context. (c) Cosine similarity between the currently generated frame and preceding frames. The consistently high similarity observed in static background regions demonstrates the potential for extensive feature reuse during computation.

Figure 3: Dynamics-guided Distribution Matching Distillation. To mitigate static bias, we introduce a dynamic weight mask based on temporal cosine similarity. By amplifying loss in high-motion regions, it penalizes static predictions and forces the model to learn complex dynamics.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion has emerged as a leading paradigm for efficient video generation, yet its practical deployment remains bottlenecked by the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency. We attribute this bottleneck to three error sources in AR rollouts: the base model error, the train-inference distribution mismatch, and the upstream error propagation. Building on this decomposition, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the per-step and cumulative errors, providing a principled basis for jointly optimizing generation quality and inference efficiency. Guided by this analysis, we propose TriTD, a Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution co-optimized distillation framework with three complementary modules. First, for ODE initialization, we adopt a Next-Node Trajectory Distillation (NTD) objective, which shortens the supervision horizon and admits a lower regression-error floor. Second, we introduce Chunk-Graded Noising (CGN), a monotonically non-decreasing per-chunk noising schedule that helps narrow the expected train-inference noise mismatch and removes redundant KV-cache updates, yielding substantial speedups at no quality cost. Third, we propose Orthogonal-Parallel DMD (OP-DMD), a distribution-matching loss that retains the original DMD supervision while introducing an additional regression constraint in the orthogonal subspace to suppress off-axis drift, improving both training stability and final generation quality. Extensive experiments show that TriTD consistently surpasses existing baselines in visual quality while reaching a real-time throughput of 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU, delivering a balanced quality-efficiency solution for interactive streaming video generation.
authors: Jia Li, Xurui Peng, Haowei Zhu, Tianyu Zhao, Jiexi Wang, Youwei Zheng, Yuxi Ren, Xinglong Wu, Xing Wang, Hayden Kwok-Hay So
bullets: Targets three AR rollout issues: base-model error, train–inference distribution mismatch, and upstream error propagation.
Derives closed-form bounds for per-step and cumulative errors to guide quality–efficiency optimization.
Combines Next-Node Trajectory Distillation, Chunk-Graded Noising, and Orthogonal-Parallel DMD.
Chunk-Graded Noising reduces redundant KV-cache updates without sacrificing quality, while OP-DMD improves stability and generation quality.
Experiments report consistent visual-quality gains over existing baselines and real-time throughput for interactive streaming video generation.

papers.abstract: Video generation models synthesize visual sequences from text and image inputs. Extending video generation to long animations requires actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments to remain coordinated across scenes. Executable scene programs make these decisions available for inspection. Constructing an entire story before observing its execution can leave later scenes dependent on unrealized events. We present SpriteStage, a progressive scene programming framework that builds animation through iterative enactment and engine reorchestration. Iterative enactment generates each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, executes it on a shared spatial stage, and uses runtime and visual feedback to revise the relevant actions or story beats. The accepted outcome becomes the starting state for the next scene. Engine reorchestration maps the resulting draft to production assets and engine capabilities while retaining its events, geometry, and timing. Inspection of the assembled sequence and frozen replay carry the accepted performance into the final video. Three complete animations, ranging from approximately 9.9 to 14.3 minutes, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in producing extended narratives through scene programming and engine execution.
authors: Zhaoqi Wang, Zijian Zhang, Jiamou Liu
bullets: Targets the coordination of actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments across long animations.
Builds each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, then uses runtime and visual feedback for revision.
Reorchestrates scene drafts onto production assets and engine capabilities while preserving events, geometry, and timing.
Uses sequence inspection and frozen replay to transfer accepted performances into the final video.
Demonstrated through three complete animations lasting approximately 9.9–14.3 minutes.

Fig. 2. Iterative enactment in SpriteStage. Runtime and visual feedback guide scene acceptance, local repair, and broader revision. Accepted world and narrative states guide the next scene.

papers.tldr: SpriteStage generates long-form animations by progressively scripting, executing, inspecting, and revising scenes while carrying accepted world states forward.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two alternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator's intermediate features to estimate each token's remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing preserves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ~1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5x faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ~2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35x faster at 24.5 fps.
authors: Hyunwook Choi, Seungryong Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Uniformly denoising every token to the final step wastes computation because some tokens stabilize early.
The method treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and uses verifiers to decide when tokens can be accepted and frozen.
Frozen tokens stop denoising while their cached keys and values remain available as context for later tokens.
Two verifiers are explored: a training-free similarity-and-stability test and a learned feature-based predictor of remaining error.
It preserves full-step quality while reducing computation, achieving over 1.5× speedup on LongLive and 1.35× on Lingbot-World 2.0.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparisons on video generation and world modeling. Both our head and training-free verifiers preserve visual quality comparable to the four-step baseline without visibly increasing quality drift over the illustrated rollouts on our benchmark.

Figure 3: Speculative Forcing. Baseline runs every token through the full denoising schedule. Speculative Forcing instead treats each token’s intermediate clean estimate as a draft and asks a verifier to predict its remaining gap relk(i) to the full-step output. Tokens predicted to have converged are accepted and committed, after which they enter the next step only as keys and values, so the following denoising pass is computed for the rejected tokens alone.

Figure 2: Token-wise convergence during denoising. We visualize latent differences between each chunk’s k-step prediction and the baseline four-step output. (a) In video generation, background and object regions that remain similar to history tend to converge early, while other regions continue to change. (b) In world generation, previously observed regions often converge early, whereas newly revealed regions tend to require further denoising.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation underlies real-time, causal video synthesis and is the backbone of video world models. Today's dominant approach distills a bidirectional diffusion model into a causal few-step student, but existing pipelines make this conversion prohibitively expensive, requiring offline Probability Flow ODE} (PF-ODE) trajectories that cost tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of storage. We show it can be made dramatically more efficient. Pushing this efficiency to its extreme, we reduce trajectory supervision to a single sample, the strictest setting possible, and find that it causes severe quality collapse. We trace this to the teacher's trajectory geometry: the high-noise regime, governing semantic layout and motion, and the low-noise regime, governing fine texture exhibit fundamentally different curvature and optimization behavior, so a single monolithic student cannot jointly fit both, causing severe representation interference. Motivated by this, we propose Glance Forcing, a lightweight distillation framework that decouples the denoising trajectory into two complementary slow and fast experts, each guided by a tailored, stage-specific objective, while keeping the pretrained teacher entirely frozen. This decoupling further reveals a general mechanism underlying few-step distillation: PF-ODE distillation mainly straightens the few-step trajectory geometry, while the subsequent distribution-matching stage independently governs distributional quality. Using only one PF-ODE trajectory, Glance Forcing already surpasses the fully-trained state-of-the-art baseline, raising the VBench Total score from 84.04 to 84.22 while cutting trajectory-collection cost from thousands of GPU-hours to about one A100-GPU-hour, with markedly larger gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, and instruction-following, and consistent preference from human raters over strong baselines.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Junchao Yi, Hu Jian Guo, Linjie Li, Rui Zhao, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Existing causal distillation pipelines require tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of PF-ODE trajectory data.
The authors attribute single-sample quality collapse to different optimization geometry in high-noise semantic/motion and low-noise texture regimes.
Glance Forcing uses two frozen-teacher-guided slow and fast experts with stage-specific objectives to decouple these regimes.
With one PF-ODE trajectory, it raises VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.22 and reduces trajectory collection to about one A100-GPU-hour.
It also reports gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, instruction following, and human preference over strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Xiaobing Tu, Xiantao Zhang, Jinkui Ren, Yinggui Wang, Yue Ma, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high latency and non-causal processing of existing video object removal methods.
Transfers erasing capability from a text-to-video foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser.
Uses sliding-window causal attention, attention sinks, self-rollout, and KV-cache rolling to maintain fixed-context, constant-speed generation.
Reports sub-second latency and up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU.
Introduces the LongErase benchmark and supports interactive, infinite-length video erasing with strong real-world generalization.

papers.abstract: Distilling pretrained video diffusion models into few-step autoregressive (AR) generators typically combines student initialization with distribution matching distillation (DMD). An intermediate AR teacher can provide causally compatible targets for ODE initialization. However, causally compatible targets alone do not ensure high-quality generation under a short sampling schedule. We analyze the posterior-mean predictions favored by direct latent regression and empirically find that causal ODE initialization alleviates blur but still leaves fine detail unresolved. To address this limitation, we propose Representation Forcing, which learns few-step causal initialization through representation-space supervision rather than intermediate-teacher trajectory regression. The student is trained with teacher forcing by comparing clean predictions and training targets through normalized features of a frozen video diffusion transformer. This phase reuses the synthetic videos generated by a bidirectional model for AR teacher training and replaces both teacher training and causal ODE distillation, without generating additional causal ODE trajectories. The subsequent asymmetric DMD procedure remains unchanged. Empirical results show that, at four sampling steps, RepForcing better preserves generation quality than intermediate-teacher-based initialization before DMD. After DMD, our four-step chunk-wise model improves VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.66 (+0.62 points) and VisionReward from 6.326 to 10.074 (+59.25%) over the reported causal-ODE-based baseline.
authors: Siming Fu, Zheming Fu, Lianrui Mu, Haoyang Huang, Chaojie Gu, Ruizhe He
bullets: Causal ODE initialization reduces blur but can leave fine details unresolved under short sampling schedules.
RepForcing uses teacher forcing to match clean predictions and targets through normalized features from a frozen video diffusion transformer.
It reuses synthetic videos from bidirectional-model training and avoids additional causal ODE trajectory generation.
At four sampling steps, it better preserves quality before DMD than intermediate-teacher initialization.
After DMD, it raises VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.66 and VisionReward from 6.326 to 10.074 over the reported causal-ODE baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Representation Forcing Initialization Pipeline. Training videos are encoded into clean latent blocks by a VAE encoder. The trainable causal DiT reconstructs clean blocks from noisy inputs, conditioned on preceding clean blocks under teacher forcing. The predicted and target video latents are passed separately through the same truncated, frozen Wan2.1-14B to obtain features f̂ and f . A token-wise cosine loss compares these features, with stop-gradient (sg) on the target branch. Gradients propagate through the frozen extractor to update the causal DiT. This initialization replaces intermediate AR teacher training and causal ODE distillation.

(2026); frame-wise four-step Causal Forcing++ scores come from its own report (Zhao et al., 2026), and Causal-rCM scores are obtained from evaluations of pretrained weights (Zheng et al., 2026).

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a foundation for long-horizon world rollout. However, when extended far beyond their training windows, these models suffer from progressive drift: visual quality deteriorates, motion becomes inconsistent, and object identity gradually collapses as generated frames are recursively reused as context. We study a supervision-horizon gap: short-horizon distillation leaves later rollout states without direct supervision. We show that matching short-window marginals need not determine long-horizon behavior, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to training. This motivates temporal manifold matching at scale for long-horizon world models. Building on this insight, we introduce LongForcing, a distillation approach that scales teacher supervision to long student self-rollouts. LongForcing preserves the short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, while replacing the realscore teacher in the final distribution-matching stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. The long-horizon teacher supervises extended student self-rollouts using the standard distribution-matching formulation, without modifying the student architecture or increasing inference cost. We evaluate LongForcing on text-to-video generation and interactive action-conditioned world models, achieving a VBench Quality score of 85.52 and improving WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests further sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours, far beyond the training horizon. These results suggest that scaling supervision along the temporal axis is a practical step toward long-horizon world models. The project website and code are at https://github.com/Fantasy-AMAP/LongForcing.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Mengchao Wang, Junfeng Ni, Ting-Bing Xu, Zhicheng Liu, Mu Xu
bullets: Targets progressive visual degradation, motion inconsistency, and object-identity collapse beyond the training horizon.
Identifies a supervision-horizon gap: short-window distillation does not constrain delayed rollout failures.
Extends temporal manifold matching by replacing the final-stage realscore teacher with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher.
Preserves the student architecture and inference cost while supervising long self-rollouts.
Reports a VBench Quality score of 85.52, a 23.9-point improvement on the WorldRoamBench 60s action score in first-person ablations, and qualitative rollouts up to 24 hours.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
authors: Xiaoxue Wu, Xinyu Gao, Fang Yu, Yu Qiao, Xinyuan Chen
bullets: Targets redundant, frame-level memory retrieval that gives all query tokens the same historical context.
Organizes historical KV-cache tokens into online semantic clusters guided by attention patterns.
Uses query-adaptive, fine-grained retrieval to broaden historical access under a fixed memory budget.
Improves long-range and inter-shot consistency, especially when earlier content is revisited, while approximating full-memory access.
Introduces VLM-assisted metrics for evaluating faithful consistency across shots; experiments support the framework’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CineMem. Existing autoregressive video generation methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level, which may result in redundant retrieval, inefficient memory utilization, and overlooked heterogeneous information needs across query tokens. CineMem combines an online-clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval to enable a finer-grained memory retrieval strategy. As illustrated by the attention receptive fields, CineMem provides broader (2/3 vs. 12/12) access to historical information under the same retrieval budget.

Figure 3: Our memory retrieval framework. Through multi-stage initial adaptation, we convert a bidirectional model into an autoregressive multi-shot model with memory retrieval. During inference, queries access memory from the first chunk, adjacent chunk, and retrieved candidates via token-wise and head-wise retrieval. Previous adjacent chunks are progressively integrated into retrieval candidates through online KV-cache clustering with cluster balancing. During training, resampling ground truth frames provides memory inputs to alleviate error accumulation.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results. We compare CineMem with representative causal and bidirectional baselines on 15s multi-shot video generation. Representative examples illustrate the qualitative improvements of our method.
Figure 6: Implementation of PTCS. PTCS assigns low scores when either unchanged semantic elements are not preserved or intended changes are not correctly realized.

Figure 4: Intrinsic memory-selection patterns under the full-memory setting. Memory tokens exhibit semantically meaningful clustering structures, while different query-head pairs show distinct preferences over memory tokens. Although each query-head pair selects a subset of the most relevant tokens, their union covers nearly the entire memory. See Appendix A for more details.

Figure 10: Visualization of token clustering before and after RoPE. Compared with Pre-RoPE representations, Post-RoPE similarities exhibit stronger positional dependency and weaker semantic clustering structures.

Figure 9: Comparison of memory-token coverage and selection overlap under three selection granularities: query-head-wise, query-wise with head averaging, and head-wise with query averaging. The horizontal axis denotes the fraction of memory tokens selected by each selection unit. The left panel reports the percentage of distinct memory-token positions covered by the union of all selections, while the right panel shows the percentage of selected positions with multiplicity at least two.

Figure 11: Precision (left) and recall (right) of different retrieval strategies under varying fullmemory attention thresholds. For each query-head pair, full-memory attention serves as the oracle, and retrieved tokens are considered matched if they fall within the top-x% oracle-ranked memory tokens. Online-clustered KV cache retrieves tokens from query-specific selected clusters, while Latent-group, Frame-group, and Sliding Window perform frame-level or fixed-context retrieval. All curves are averaged over attention blocks. Online-clustered KV cache achieves a better precision-recall trade-off, providing a selective approximation to full-memory access.

Figure 7: Visualization of query-wise memory selection diversity. For the selected memory frames, different queries exhibit distinct spatial preferences within the same frame, revealing heterogeneous memory selection behaviors. Each query corresponds to the first latent of the current chunk, and each memory unit is formed by grouping neighboring 3× 3 spatial tokens.

Figure 8: Visualization of head-wise memory selection diversity. For the selected memory frames, different attention heads exhibit distinct memory preferences. We visualize multiple query regions for generality. The variations among highlighted regions across rows in each heatmap illustrate the diversity of head-wise memory selection.
Figure 15: A case of qualitative result of ablation study.
Figure 16: Distribution of evaluation prompts across different content categories, shot counts, and revisit distances.

Figure 12: Practical efficiency comparison during autoregressive rollout. The left figure shows the per-chunk denoising time, and the right figure shows the peak allocated GPU memory during 42-chunk generation.
Figure 17: Cases of longer video generated by CineMem.

Figure 13: Qualitative comparison between PTCS and similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics. The examples illustrate cases where PTCS better reflects transition correctness by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes.

Figure 14: Comparison between query-wise retrieval and the query-group retrieval variant. Querywise retrieval performs independent memory retrieval for each query token, while the query-group variant recursively partitions query tokens based on intra-group content diversity. Queries with similar content preferences are assigned to the same group and share the retrieved memory.

Figure 18: A failure case in complex multi-entity scenarios. Although the generated video preserves revisitation consistency across shots, inconsistencies such as character disappearance and detail changes occur during the transition from Shot 1 to Shot 2. This example highlights the difficulty of handling multi-entity reasoning and spatial relationship preservation in autoregressive video generation.

papers.title: CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation enables long-horizon synthesis but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate computation, yet existing controllers often couple two decisions: when to synchronize the cache exactly and how much computation to repair between synchronizations. We introduce Frequency-Step Cache (FSC), which separates these roles. FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.
authors: Kerry Xu, Param Misra, Zachary Stenglein, Athri Karunamurthy, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeated diffusion-transformer passes in long-horizon autoregressive video generation.
Uses dense-to-sparse exact-computation anchors for synchronization and frequency-resolved drift plus token age to select repair intensity.
Supports whole-step reuse, selective token recomputation, or full repair; whole-step reuse drives most speedup, while selective computation mainly restores fidelity.
On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed achieves 2.36× speedup with +0.019 SSIM and +0.5 dB PSNR over MotionCache; FSC-Quality improves matched-speed quality, including +0.031 SSIM and +1.0 dB PSNR.
Transfers without retuning to SkyReels-V2 14B and shows benefits on FramePack and Matrix-Game.

SkyReels-V2, controlled profiling setting (App. A.1): (a) 14B; (b)–(d) 1.3B. Anchor counts differ because each panel is a separate controlled study. (a) Relative-L2 error from reusing each block’s previous-step residual (band: interquartile range over blocks and prompts). (b) SSIM vs. same-seed vanilla for three placements of 7 (8 for uniform) exact anchors: dense-to-sparse (D2S, 0.861) outperforms uniform (0.856) and sparse-to-dense (S2D, 0.830). (c) Speedup vs. token fraction q. True sparse kernels reach 1.94× at q=0.10, far below their compute-proportional 2.72×; the dense-forward token-refresh reference stays at ≈ 1.23× by design (dashed: its ideal). Whole-step D2S reuse reaches 2.62×. (d) SSIM vs. speedup for anchor policies (“clean” circles: exact anchors; “approximate”: ▽ pyramid kernels,△ block-skip gates, ♢ other variants). papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.

papers.abstract: Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor-Transport-Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding-step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same-timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence-aware scheduler further adjusts the quality-efficiency trade-off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to $1.89\times$ over the original 4-step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81-frame training videos to 333-frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators synthesize long videos through chunk-wise rollouts, yet they are typically trained to predict only the immediate future. This limited prediction horizon makes it challenging to maintain video quality over extended rollouts. To address this problem, we introduce Prospective Forcing, a multi-head prediction framework that injects long-range predictive signals into autoregressive video representations. Built on a rolling-window generator, Prospective Forcing attaches lightweight, offset-specific heads that share the same conditioning information and independently predict chunks at different future temporal offsets. By extending supervision beyond the next chunk, these heads encourage the shared history representation to retain information useful for longer-horizon prediction, supporting temporally consistent generation. At inference time, we accelerate sampling by using accepted future-chunk predictions to skip full-window backbone executions. We equip the head with learnable embeddings to generate multiple candidates for the next chunk, and a learned verifier either selects a candidate or rejects all and falls back to standard autoregressive generation.

papers.abstract: In autoregressive video generation, retaining all historical key-value (KV) states increases memory usage and per-step attention costs as videos grow longer. A fixed cache budget bounds these costs but raises the challenge of preserving historical content that supports consistent, high-quality generation. Existing methods control cache size through history selection or consolidation, yet deciding what to retain and how to limit the loss of useful content remains a shared challenge. Our analysis shows that spatial queries depend on different historical content and that higher current attention coverage does not necessarily yield better long-video quality. We introduce FrameFold, a training-free KV cache consolidation method that compares the content retrieved by the same recent historical queries before and after merging to guide both representative construction and merge selection. Exploiting temporal redundancy between adjacent historical entries, FrameFold merges their KV states into shared representatives while retaining complete spatial grids. It fits value-merging coefficients in closed form by matching conditional attention responses, then selects the merge with the lowest remaining response distortion. Under matched KV cache budgets, experiments on Self Forcing and Causal Forcing at 30 and 60 seconds and on LongLive at 120 seconds demonstrate improved consistency and visual quality. Continuous eight-minute Self Forcing rollouts further show less quality degradation than the baselines.
authors: Muyu Liu, Mingming Liu, Hong Gu, Yuyao Zhang, Qin Lu
bullets: Fixed-size KV caches reduce memory and attention costs but risk discarding content needed for temporal consistency.

Value-merging coefficients are solved in closed form, and merges are selected to minimize response distortion.
Experiments across 30-second to eight-minute rollouts show better consistency, visual quality, and slower degradation than baselines under matched cache budgets.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation models generate videos sequentially, with each new block conditioned on previously generated blocks. By training on the model's own rollouts, Self Forcing and its follow-up methods substantially mitigate exposure bias caused by the mismatch between training- and inference-time history distributions. However, these models still suffer from error accumulation during long-horizon generation. We identify a key underlying limitation: the model remains highly sensitive to errors in its generated history, allowing small deviations to be amplified through subsequent generations. We refer to this underexplored problem as the local history robustness gap. To address this gap, we introduce Adversarial Gradient Forcing (AGF), a framework designed to improve the robustness of few-step autoregressive video models to perturbations and accumulated errors in their own generated histories. AGF uses distribution matching gradients from future block predictions to select adversarial perturbations of self-generated histories. It then jointly trains the generator on the original and perturbed histories to improve the robustness of future generation. Extensive experiments show that AGF achieves the highest VBench Total score on 60-second video generation and the best visual quality on four-minute video generation. Notably, AGF achieves such long-horizon robustness while requiring only 5-second rollouts for training.

Achieves long-horizon robustness while training with only 5-second rollouts.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models maintain a growing attention key-value (KV) cache, making memory a key bottleneck for long video generation. Recently, clustering-based quantization has emerged as an effective method to compress video KV caches by grouping similar key and value vectors then quantizing residual errors. However, when later frames attend to the compressed history, small reconstruction errors can compound as the video grows. Beyond the within-layer similarity exploited by clustering, we find strong dependencies across cache layers in video models. This motivates Coral-KV - Calibrated Offline, Residual-coded, and Adapted Locally - a KV-cache compression framework that uses cache states in each layer to predict keys and values in subsequent layers, then quantizes the remaining prediction residuals. We construct compact block-diagonal-plus-low-rank (block-DPLR) predictors: block-diagonal components model channel relationships within each attention head, while a global low-rank term models dependencies between heads. Coral-KV exposes a flexible fidelity-memory trade-off: it can reuse its predictors across videos or refit lightweight block-diagonal predictors to the current video for higher fidelity. Across extensive evaluations on both HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1, our reusable configuration improves PSNR over QVG-4 by 0.32 dB and 4.95 dB, respectively, while using 48% and 37% less cache memory. Against QVG-Pro, our video-adapted configuration improves MAGI-1 PSNR by 3.77 dB while using 33.7% less cache memory. Coral-KV also maintains higher reconstruction fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities while retaining comparable generation latency.

Supports reusable predictors for efficiency or lightweight video-specific refitting for higher fidelity.
Improves PSNR while reducing cache memory versus QVG-4 and QVG-Pro across HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1.
Maintains fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities with comparable latency.

papers.abstract: To stream long videos while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency, Self Forcing mitigates exposure bias through self-rollout training on self-generated histories with key-value (KV) caching. To keep memory manageable, it detaches historical caches, preserving forward dependencies between chunks but severing the backward gradient paths. We introduce Connected Self Forcing, a training framework that reconnects gradient paths across autoregressive chunks, allowing feedback from later predictions to guide how earlier context is generated. These connections go beyond historical KV-writing: gradients pass through generated latents into the computations that produced them, linking the generation of earlier context to its use in later predictions. To make this connected training memory-efficient, we develop shortcut gradient replay, which recovers cross-chunk gradients without retaining the full rollout computation graph. Integrated with distribution matching distillation, Connected Self Forcing trains historical chunks according to both their direct supervision and their contribution to subsequent generation. Experiments on autoregressive video generation show improvements in long-horizon visual quality and temporal consistency, without changing the inference procedure.
authors: Dongbin Zhang, Chaoda Zheng, Kangjie Chen, Xiangyu Li, Shijia Chen, Jinhao Deng, Yuqi Zhang, Guangfeng Jiang, Hongbin Lin, Choo Sin Wai, Minqi Wang, Puyi Wang, Jingye Zhang, Yu Zhang, Xianming Liu, Boyang Wang
bullets: Addresses exposure bias and weak long-range learning caused by detached historical KV caches in Self Forcing.
Reconnects gradient paths across autoregressive chunks, including through generated latents and the computations that produced them.
Introduces shortcut gradient replay to recover cross-chunk gradients without storing the full rollout graph.
Combines connected training with distribution matching distillation, supervising chunks based on both direct accuracy and downstream impact.
Experiments report improved long-horizon visual quality and temporal consistency without modifying inference.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Connected Self Forcing. Self Forcing uses detached autoregressive rollouts, where each generated chunk x̂i receives only direct DMD supervision. Connected Self Forcing restores cross-chunk feedback through Shortcut Gradient Replay: gradients from a later prediction are replayed to historical KV states KVj , then propagated through the KV writer GKV θ and generator Gθ, which share parameters θ. Replay stops at earlier generated history to avoid recursive backpropagation through the earlier generation branches. This trains each chunk both for its own generation quality and as context for subsequent generation, without adding parameters or changing inference.

This suggests that gradient components opposing the direct DMD objective are not necessarily purely detrimental. One possible interpretation is that part of the negative-direction feedback from gcross acts as a damping signal, encouraging more conservative temporal evolution and thereby reducing motion dynamics. papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion enables causal video streaming without a bidirectional pass over the full clip, but existing few-step systems usually retain only the opening and most recent frames in a fixed-size KV cache. Once an event leaves this window, later frames can no longer attend to it, a failure we term mid-horizon forgetting. We present Memory Forcing, a few-step streaming method that preserves this missing history without increasing the cache size. Its Archive \& Working Banks partition the cache into sink, archive, and working regions, retaining diverse intermediate events alongside recent motion under fixed memory. Because absolute temporal indices drift outside the training range, Bank-aware RoPE reassigns indices at attention time so each bank remains distinguishable. At 1.3B, Memory Forcing leads on longer clips, shows the smallest drop from 5s to 60s among methods reporting all four lengths, and preserves subjects and scenes through leave-and-return. The same design scales to Wan2.2 5B, producing more physically plausible, realistic, and dynamic videos and, to our knowledge, the first public 5B model on this forcing line.
authors: Jiaming Zhang, Xinyu Wang, Huafeng Shi, Gangshan Wu, Limin Wang
bullets: Existing streaming systems typically retain only initial and recent frames, so intermediate events become inaccessible over long clips.
Archive and Working Banks divide the cache into sink, archive, and working regions to retain both past events and recent motion without increasing memory.
Bank-aware RoPE remaps temporal indices at attention time so the separate memory banks remain distinguishable beyond the training range.
At 1.3B, the method performs strongly on longer clips, with the smallest reported 5s-to-60s degradation among comparable methods.
Scaling to Wan2.2 5B yields more physically plausible, realistic, and dynamic videos, including subject and scene continuity through leave-and-return events.

papers.abstract: Causal video diffusion models generate video autoregressively, which suits streaming, interactive, and long-video generation. Under standard training, however, they often yield lower generation quality than bidirectional models of the same size. Many existing approaches address this gap by initializing from or distilling a pretrained bidirectional teacher. We instead train a causal model from an image-model initialization, with no bidirectional video model at any stage. Because this path requires neither a large bidirectional teacher nor a complex distillation pipeline, it is simpler and more scalable. On this path, we find that a causal model trained on ground-truth history becomes strongly dependent on it, so that at inference errors in its own generated history propagate forward. We hypothesize that much of this dependence is unnecessary, because the current input already determines much of what the history provides. We propose Conditional Residual Prediction (CRP), a simple recipe for reducing a model's reliance on a condition: the model first predicts the target without the condition, and the condition may only add a residual on top of this prediction. Applied to history, CRP makes the model predict each chunk from the present as far as it can and use the past only for what the present cannot supply. In controlled experiments, CRP nearly closes the 6.14-point gap to a bidirectional model trained under the same setup. Scaling this recipe, we train Optica, a 2B-parameter causal video model that autoregressively generates 5-second 480p videos and reaches 82.78 on VBench with only about 15M training videos.
authors: Bowen Zheng, Zhiguang Liu, Jiarong Ou, Rui Chen, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Causal video models support streaming and long-video generation but can underperform same-size bidirectional models because prediction errors accumulate through generated history.
The authors train from an image-model initialization, avoiding pretrained bidirectional video models and complex distillation pipelines.
CRP first predicts each video chunk without historical context, then uses the history only to add a residual for information the current input cannot provide.
In controlled experiments, CRP nearly closes a 6.14-point quality gap to a matched bidirectional model.
The resulting 2B-parameter Optica model generates 5-second 480p videos and scores 82.78 on VBench using about 15M training videos.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Overview. (a) Conditional Residual Prediction (CRP) applied to history. The same network 𝑓𝜃 is evaluated twice on the same input: the History-Free branch masks out the history and predicts 𝑥free, and the History-Conditioned branch sees the history and predicts only a residual 𝑥cond on top of it. The History-Free hidden states are detached and added to the History-Conditioned branch after every block, never the reverse, so the History-Free branch stays free of history. (b) A video VAE encodes the first frame into its own latent and every later four frames into one, with causal temporal convolutions that entangle latents across time. papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation requires denoising the current frames while writing their key-value representations as context for future predictions. However, these two roles typically share parameters, and we find that their gradients exhibit distinct patterns and systematic negative alignment, hindering the joint optimization of visual quality and temporal consistency. We introduce Self Gradient Forcing Plus (SGF+), which assigns separate parameters to context writing and denoising while preserving their interaction through causal attention. Both roles are jointly optimized using the original generation objective without auxiliary losses, with context writing supervised through its contribution to future predictions. This simple change improves visual quality and long-horizon consistency over the evaluated baselines in both framewise and chunkwise generation, without additional video training data or a longer training horizon. Trained on only 5s rollouts, SGF+ supports continuous generation for up to 24 hours without long-video fine-tuning. These results highlight role-specific parameterization as an effective design principle for high-quality autoregressive video generation and native long-horizon extrapolation.
bullets: Shared parameters for denoising and future-context writing produce conflicting gradients that hinder joint optimization.
SGF+ gives each role separate parameters while retaining causal-attention interaction.
Both roles use the original generation objective, with context writing trained through its impact on future predictions.
The method improves visual quality and long-horizon consistency in framewise and chunkwise generation over evaluated baselines.
Despite training on 5-second rollouts, it enables continuous generation for up to 24 hours without long-video fine-tuning.

SGF accumulates contextwriting and denoising gradients on shared parameters θ, whereas SGF+ assigns separate parameters θc and θd to the two roles.

papers.abstract: Bidirectional video diffusion models denoise entire videos in parallel, yet when trained on effectively unlimited in-distribution data from procedural generators, continue to violate physical laws and simple symbolic rules. We introduce Serial-to-Parallel Diffusion (S2PD), which performs autoregressive diffusion at high noise before switching to parallel diffusion at low noise. The autoregressive phase provides the serial computation needed to coordinate interdependent events and produce valid state transitions while the parallel phase jointly refines the entire video and reduces sampling time relative to fully serial generation. We implement S2PD with two architectures: a pixel-space diffusion transformer trained from scratch and a pretrained video model adapted through LoRA fine-tuning with causal attention. Across games, physical simulations, and real video, S2PD follows rules more reliably than matched bidirectional baselines and generates videos with greater temporal stability and sampling efficiency than other serial methods.
authors: Jeffrey Hu, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Ayush Tewari
bullets: Bidirectional video diffusion can violate physical laws and symbolic rules even with abundant procedural training data.
S2PD uses autoregressive diffusion at high noise to coordinate dependent events and valid state transitions.
It switches to parallel diffusion at low noise to jointly refine the video and improve sampling efficiency.
The approach is implemented with a pixel-space diffusion transformer and a LoRA-adapted pretrained video model with causal attention.
Across games, physical simulations, and real video, S2PD is reported to improve rule adherence and temporal stability versus matched bidirectional and other serial baselines.
